name: The Human Review Rule
title: The Human Review Rule
answer: The Human Review Rule says AI can inform a decision about a child or an employee, but a named person must make the decision. The district writes down which decisions always require human review, adopts that list at the board level, and checks each year that the rule is followed. It matters because daily scores and flags can quietly turn into decisions unless a person is clearly accountable.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: The idea is a policy that names the decisions which cannot be left to an AI tool alone. The list should cover grades, special education decisions, discipline, placement, teacher evaluation, threat assessment, and hiring. It solves the problem of a rule that exists only in principle and then fades once tools produce scores and flags every day. The chapter turns the earlier rule into something a district can adopt, follow, and audit. The review process itself matters, because how a person reviews an AI suggestion affects whether errors are caught.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The district writes the list of decisions that must pass through a person and adopts it at the board level. A named person makes each decision, and the AI may only inform it. The person should record their own judgment before looking at the AI's suggestion, because the order of review matters, and Figure 3.5 turns this into four steps. Each year a small team pulls a sample of decisions and checks whether a person actually reviewed each one. The text does not give separate grade bands for this practice, so the rule applies across the listed decisions rather than by grade level.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book's evidence for this idea is a set of experiments in which people asked to correct a machine's decision often went along with bad decisions, while people who decided first and then saw the machine's view corrected mistakes (Krugel et al., 2023). The text does not attach a separate evidence label to this finding. It uses the finding to argue that schools should have the person record their own judgment before seeing the AI's suggestion. Figure 3.5 turns that lesson into four steps. The annual audit is presented as the practice that keeps the rule from fading, not as a research finding.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main risk is that a rule on paper fades in practice. Once a tool produces scores and flags every day, it becomes easy to treat those outputs as decisions. The annual audit is the safeguard: a small team pulls a sample of decisions each year and checks whether a person actually reviewed each one. The decisions that stay with a person include grades, special education decisions, discipline, placement, teacher evaluation, threat assessment, and hiring. AI may inform those decisions, but a named person makes them, and the person's own judgment should be recorded before the AI's suggestion is seen.
